metadata.note: The other half of the Pere Marquette system: the Chicago and West Michigan Railway heritage, covering the Lake Michigan shoreline south of Ludington (see flint_pere_marquette_mainline.geojson for the Flint-Ludington namesake mainline). The Chicago and Michigan Lake Shore Railroad, chartered 1869, opened New Buffalo-St. Joseph (27 miles) Feb 1 1870, then extended up the lakeshore: Grand Junction Feb 28 1871, Montague Jul 1 1871, and Pentwater Jan 1 1872 (169.8 miles New Buffalo-Pentwater). Two branches opened the same era: Holland-Grand Rapids (built by the separate Grand Rapids and Holland Railroad) on Jan 1 1872, and Muskegon-Big Rapids in 1873. Falling revenue pushed the company into receivership in late 1876; it reorganized as the Chicago and West Michigan Railroad on Dec 28 1878, consolidating these lines (and, by 1881, the separate Grand Rapids, Newaygo and Lake Shore Railroad) into one system. Chicago and West Michigan then merged with the Flint and Pere Marquette Railway and the Detroit, Grand Rapids and Western Railway in 1900 to form the Pere Marquette Railroad, and the Chesapeake and Ohio Railway fully absorbed Pere Marquette in 1947. Geometry is a real-town waypoint approximation, straight-line segments between documented stations -- NOT digitized from period track maps. COLOR NOTE: every feature here that was actually part of the Pere Marquette Railroad (1900-1947) uses color #9C6644, matching every other Pere Marquette-branded feature across this entire map (see flint_pere_marquette_mainline.geojson, thumb_michigan_railroads.geojson, and detroit_flint.geojson) -- the goal is that any line ever operated by Pere Marquette reads as the same color wherever it appears. Pre-1900 predecessor-company eras and the post-1947 C&O era keep their own distinct colors, since those were different operators. GEOMETRY FIXED (2026-08-23): the New Buffalo-Pentwater lakeshore geometry originally jumped straight from Grand Junction to Montague (a ~70-mile chord with no intermediate points), cutting directly across Lake Michigan's coastal bulge instead of following the shore -- visibly wrong on the rendered map. Added South Haven, Saugatuck, Holland, and Grand Haven as real coastal-town waypoints along that stretch, all towns the actual lakeshore line is understood to have passed through, though the exact original station list for this specific segment is not independently confirmed (see not_yet_sourced).
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_and_Michigan_Lake_Shore_Railroad (chartered 1869; New Buffalo-St. Joseph opened Feb 1 1870; extended to Grand Junction Feb 28 1871, Montague Jul 1 1871, Pentwater Jan 1 1872, 169.8 miles total; Holland-Grand Rapids branch via the Grand Rapids and Holland Railroad opened Jan 1 1872; Muskegon-Big Rapids branch opened 1873; receivership late 1876; reorganized as Chicago and West Michigan Railroad Dec 28 1878)

metadata.not_yet_sourced: Exact discontinuation dates for passenger service on any of these three corridors specifically (all approximated at Amtrak's May 1 1971 creation, matching this map's convention for Michigan branch lines not selected by Amtrak, not independently confirmed); precise frequency for any era, all estimated; the Grand Rapids, Newaygo and Lake Shore Railroad's own route is not separately modeled here, only noted as folded into the 1881 consolidation.
metadata.line_label_audit: 2026-08-24: line labels normalised repo-wide to "<operating company>: <line name>" -- the company's common display name (legal suffixes dropped), then the line as a passenger would have known it, or its two terminals where the line carried no advertised name. Long intermediate station lists were reduced to endpoints. For features spanning several operators the company shown is the one that ran the line for most of its drawn years. See CLAUDE.md Rule 6.
